skills.name: benchmarking
skills.description: Guide for building, running, and analyzing Nanvix performance benchmarks. Use this when asked about benchmark setup, execution, or interpretation.

skills.name: build
skills.description: Guide for building, formatting, linting, and spell-checking Nanvix with z. Use this when asked to build or validate the repository.

skills.name: ci-cd-pipeline
skills.description: Guide for Nanvix CI and GitHub Actions workflow behavior, including local pipeline execution and matrix coverage. Use this when asked about CI checks, workflow failures, or release flow.

skills.name: coding-standards
skills.description: Detailed Nanvix coding, documentation, and review standards across Rust, C/C++, Python, and Shell. Use this when asked to implement or review code quality conventions.

skills.name: daemon-development
skills.description: Guide for developing and debugging Nanvix daemons, including guest daemons and host linuxd behavior. Use this when asked about daemon architecture or daemon changes.

skills.name: gdb-debugging
skills.description: Guide for debugging Nanvix guests using GDB remote debugging over the microvm machine type. Use this when asked about attaching GDB, setting breakpoints, or stepping through kernel code.

skills.name: kernel-development
skills.description: Guide for modifying and debugging the Nanvix kernel architecture and kernel-call paths. Use this when asked about kernel internals or kernel implementation changes.

skills.name: library-development
skills.description: Guide for creating and modifying Nanvix libraries under src/libs, including guest no_std and host std crates. Use this when asked about library architecture or crate changes.

skills.name: test-development
skills.description: Guide for writing, running, and debugging Nanvix unit, integration, and system tests in Rust and C/C++. Use this when asked about test implementation or failures.

skills.name: test
skills.description: Guide for running Nanvix tests with z. Use this when asked to run unit tests, integration tests, or the full test suite.

skills.name: troubleshooting
skills.description: Guide for diagnosing Nanvix build, runtime, and test failures, including cleanup and debugging workflows. Use this when asked to investigate errors or unstable behavior.

skills.name: user-app-development
skills.description: Guide for developing, building, and running Nanvix user-space applications across supported runtimes and languages. Use this when asked about guest app implementation or execution.

skills.name: find-skills
skills.description: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.

Use when the user mentions copilot-setup-steps, copilot setup steps, or wants to configure the cloud agent environment.

1. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
2. use vstd::arithmetic::power2::pow2;
3. 
4. verus! {
5. 
6. // =================================================================================================
7. // Abstract models of frame-number quantities, realized by the verified `arch` crate.
8. //
9. // `FrameNumber` is a newtype defined in the `arch` crate. Its real `#[verus_spec]` contracts (a
10. // `View` giving the integer index `frame@`, and the associated bound `FrameNumber::spec_max()`)
11. // supersede the former placeholder `assume_specification`s. These helpers re-expose those arch
12. // quantities under the names the kernel proofs already use.
13. // =================================================================================================
14. 
15. // The integer index (raw value) of a frame number: its `arch` view.
16. pub open spec fn spec_frame_raw_value(frame: FrameNumber) -> int {
17.     frame@
18. }
19. 
20. // The largest representable frame index (the `arch` bound `FrameNumber::spec_max()`).
21. pub open spec fn spec_max_frame_number() -> int {
22.     FrameNumber::spec_max() as int
23. }
24. 
25. // =================================================================================================
26. // Derived spec helpers over the `PhysicalAddress` view (its `int` raw address).
27. // =================================================================================================
28. 
29. // The frame an address belongs to: `addr / FRAME_SIZE` (equivalently `addr >> FRAME_SHIFT`).
30. pub open spec fn spec_frame_number(addr_view: int) -> int {
31.     addr_view / spec_page_size()
32. }
33. 
34. // The base address of a frame: `frame_index * FRAME_SIZE`.
35. pub open spec fn spec_from_number(frame_view: int) -> int {
36.     frame_view * spec_page_size()
37. }
38. 
39. impl PhysicalAddress {
40.     // Well-formedness: the address has a representable frame number. This is exactly what makes
41.     // `into_frame_number` total (its internal `FrameNumber::from_raw_value(..).unwrap()` never
42.     // panics). `open` so callers' proofs (frame allocator, page tables) can rely on totality.
43.     pub open spec fn inv(&self) -> bool {
44.         spec_frame_number(self@) <= spec_max_frame_number()
45.     }
46. }
47. 
48. // =================================================================================================
49. // Dependency contracts for not-yet-verified modules.
50. //
51. // `VirtualAddress` (the `sys` crate) and `FRAME_SHIFT` (the `arch` crate) are not yet
52. // verified. They are given trusted external specifications so that the verified `PhysicalAddress`
53. // bodies can be translated. These declarations are placeholders: when the underlying modules are
54. // verified, their real specifications will supersede these.
55. // =================================================================================================
56. 
57. // Note: `VirtualAddress::new` now carries its own verified `#[verus_spec]` in the `sys` crate
58. // (`result@ == value as int`), so its placeholder `assume_specification` was removed — the real
59. // specification supersedes it.
60. 
61. pub assume_specification[ <::sys::mm::VirtualAddress as ::sys::mm::Address>::into_raw_value ](
62.     addr: VirtualAddress,
63. ) -> (result: usize)
64.     ensures
65.         result as int == addr@,
66. ;
67. 
68. // Note: `arch::mem::FRAME_SHIFT` now carries its own verified modeling in the `arch` crate
69. // (`#[verus_verify]` on the constant, transparently `PAGE_SHIFT`), so its placeholder
70. // `assume_specification` was removed — the real definition supersedes it. The facts the proofs
71. // relied on (`FRAME_SHIFT < 32` and `spec_page_size() == pow2(FRAME_SHIFT)`) now follow from the
72. // transparent constant values together with `vstd`'s `lemma2_to64` (see `into_frame_number`).
73. 
74. // Note: `FrameNumber::from_raw_value` / `into_raw_value` now carry their own verified `#[verus_spec]`
75. // contracts in the `arch` crate, so their placeholder `assume_specification`s were removed — the
76. // real specifications supersede them (see `spec_frame_raw_value` / `spec_max_frame_number` above,
77. // which now re-expose the arch quantities).
78. 
79. } // verus!
80.

1. verus! {
2. 
3. // A frame index scaled by the frame size stays within `usize`, so `from_number`'s base-address
4. // multiply never overflows. This follows from `FrameNumber::MAX == MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1`,
5. // hence `(MAX + 1) * FRAME_SIZE == MAX_ADDRESS <= usize::MAX`. Proven in the proving phase.
6. pub proof fn lemma_from_number_no_overflow(frame: FrameNumber)
7.     ensures
8.         spec_frame_raw_value(frame) * spec_page_size() <= usize::MAX as int,
9. {
10.     admit();
11. }
12. 
13. // Under `inv()`, shifting the raw address right by `FRAME_SHIFT` yields the frame index
14. // `self@ / FRAME_SIZE`, which fits a `FrameNumber`. The shift-equals-divide step uses
15. // `FRAME_SIZE == 2^FRAME_SHIFT`. Proven in the proving phase.
16. pub proof fn lemma_frame_index(
17.     addr: PhysicalAddress,
18.     raw_addr: usize,
19.     shift: usize,
20.     frame_number: usize,
21. )
22.     requires
23.         addr.inv(),
24.         raw_addr as int == addr@,
25.         shift < 64,
26.         spec_page_size() == pow2(shift as nat),
27.         frame_number == raw_addr >> shift,
28.     ensures
29.         frame_number as int == spec_frame_number(addr@),
30.         frame_number as int <= spec_max_frame_number(),
31. {
32.     admit();
33. }
34. 
35. } // verus!

35. ///
36. /// # Description
37. ///
38. /// A type that represents a physical address.
39. ///
40. #[verus_verify(external_derive)]
41. #[derive(Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord)]
42. pub struct PhysicalAddress(VirtualAddress);

46. //==================================================================================================
47. 
48. impl PhysicalAddress {
49.     pub fn from_virtual_address(addr: VirtualAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
50.         // Delegate to the per-platform validator to support sparse physical memory layouts.
51.         if !crate::hal::platform::is_valid_physical_address(addr) {
52.             return Err(Error::new(
53.                 ErrorCode::BadAddress,
54.                 "address out of bounds of physical memory",
55.             ));
56.         }
57. 
58.         Ok(Self(addr))
59.     }
60. 
61.     pub fn into_virtual_address(self) -> VirtualAddress {
62.         self.0
63.     }
64. 
65.     ///
66.     /// # Description
67.     ///
68.     /// Constructs a [`PhysicalAddress`] from a [`FrameAddress`].
69.     ///
70.     /// # Parameters
71.     ///
72.     /// - `frame_addr`: The frame address.
73.     ///
74.     /// # Returns
75.     ///
76.     /// A [`PhysicalAddress`] associated with the given `frame_addr`.
77.     ///
78.     pub fn from_frame_address(frame_addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
79.         let raw_addr: usize = frame_addr.into_raw_value() << mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
80.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(raw_addr))
81.     }
82. 
83.     pub fn from_into_frame_address(frame_addr: FrameAddress) -> Self {
84.         let raw_addr: usize = frame_addr.into_raw_value() << mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
85.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(raw_addr))
86.     }
87. }

89. // Verified conversions between a physical address, frame numbers, and MMIO addresses.
90. #[verus_verify]
91. impl PhysicalAddress {
92.     ///
93.     /// # Description
94.     ///
95.     /// Constructs a physical address from a memory-mapped I/O address.
96.     ///
97.     /// # Parameters
98.     ///
99.     /// - `addr`: The memory-mapped I/O address.
100.     ///
101.     /// # Return Values
102.     ///
103.     /// Upon success, a physical address associated with the given memory-mapped I/O address is
104.     /// returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
105.     ///
106.     /// # Safety
107.     ///
108.     /// Behavior is undefined if the provided memory-mapped I/O address is invalid.
109.     ///
110.     // Identity wrapping that deliberately bypasses the physical-RAM-range validator: MMIO
111.     // addresses may legally lie outside tracked RAM. On success the abstract address is unchanged.
112.     #[verus_spec(result =>
113.         requires
114.             spec_frame_number(addr@) <= spec_max_frame_number(),
115.         ensures
116.             result is Ok,
117.             (result->Ok_0)@ == addr@,
118.             (result->Ok_0).inv(),
119.     )]
120.     pub unsafe fn from_mmio_address(addr: VirtualAddress) -> Result<Self, Error> {
121.         Ok(Self(addr))
122.     }
123. 
124.     ///
125.     /// # Description
126.     ///
127.     /// Constructs a [`PhysicalAddress`] from a [`FrameNumber`].
128.     ///
129.     /// # Parameters
130.     ///
131.     /// - `frame`: The frame number.
132.     ///
133.     /// # Returns
134.     ///
135.     /// A [`PhysicalAddress`] associated with the given `frame_number`.
136.     ///
137.     // Total constructor: the result is the frame's base address, hence `FRAME_SIZE`-aligned.
138.     #[verus_spec(result =>
139.         ensures
140.             result@ == spec_from_number(spec_frame_raw_value(frame)),
141.     )]
142.     pub fn from_number(frame: FrameNumber) -> Self {
143.         proof! { lemma_from_number_no_overflow(frame); }
144.         let addr: usize = frame.into_raw_value() * mem::FRAME_SIZE;
145.         Self(VirtualAddress::new(addr))
146.     }
147. 
148.     // Total projection (under `inv()`): identifies the frame containing the address,
149.     // `self@ / FRAME_SIZE` (equivalently `self@ >> FRAME_SHIFT`). `inv()` underwrites the unwrap.
150.     #[verus_spec(result =>
151.         requires
152.             self.inv(),
153.         ensures
154.             spec_frame_raw_value(result) == spec_frame_number(self@),
155.     )]
156.     pub fn into_frame_number(self) -> FrameNumber {
157.         let raw_addr: usize = self.0.into_raw_value();
158.         // Bind `FRAME_SHIFT` once so the proof relates the shift below to the same value.
159.         let shift: usize = mem::FRAME_SHIFT;
160.         let frame_number: usize = raw_addr >> shift;
161.         proof! {
162.             vstd::arithmetic::power2::lemma2_to64();
163.             lemma_frame_index(self, raw_addr, shift, frame_number);
164.         }
165.         // Safety: the following unwrap is safe because a physical address has a valid frame number.
166.         FrameNumber::from_raw_value(frame_number).unwrap()
167.     }
168. }

171.     ///
172.     /// # Description
173.     ///
174.     /// Instantiates a new [`PhysicalAddress`] from a raw value.
175.     ///
176.     /// # Parameters
177.     ///
178.     /// - `raw_addr`: The raw value.
179.     ///
180.     /// # Returns
181.     ///
182.     /// - `Ok(Self)`: The new address.
183.     /// - `Err(Error::BadAddress)`: If the provided address is invalid.
184.     ///
185.     fn from_raw_value(value: usize) -> Result<Self, Error> {
186.         Self::from_virtual_address(VirtualAddress::from_raw_value(value))
187.     }

191.     ///

194.     ///
195.     /// # Parameters
196.     ///

198.     ///
199.     /// # Returns
200.     ///
201.     /// Upon success, the aligned address is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
202.     ///

204.         let aligned: VirtualAddress = self.0.align_up(align).ok_or_else(|| {
205.             let reason: &str = "align_up overflow";
206.             error!(
207.                 "PhysicalAddress::align_up(): {reason} (addr={:#x}, align={:?})",

213.         Self::from_virtual_address(aligned)
214.     }
215.

217.     /// # Description
218.     ///
219.     /// Aligns the target [`PhysicalAddress`] down to the provided `alignment`. If the address is

221.     ///

---
name: verus-constraints
description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

## Warnings

Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:

- **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
  the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
  choose triggers automatically.
- **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
  to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search

description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."
---

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

## Warnings

Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:

- **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
  the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
  choose triggers automatically.
- **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
  to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## vstd & Common Misconceptions

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

Search broadly across the entire vstd directory — do not only check one or
two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Never invent vstd functions** — verify existence in actual vstd source.
- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

## Claiming Verus Limitations

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
strengthen the proof, do not change the code.

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

---
name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. See `verus-syntax` for attribute-based syntax
reference. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function,
   following the order from the `verification-order` skill if a
   verification plan exists. Do not move to the next function until the
   current one verifies cleanly.
   
   The current module's functions must NOT have `external_body`.
   Do NOT add `external_body` to any function during proving.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Never weaken specs.** If a spec is hard to prove, the proof strategy
   is wrong — not the spec. Do not relax `requires`, weaken `ensures`,
   or remove clauses to make proofs easier. The spec is the contract.

4. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

5. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
   Trigger warnings are especially common and must not be left: add
   explicit `#[trigger]` annotations or restructure quantifiers until
   all trigger warnings are gone.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`,
  cfg-gated exec code; all must be resolved in current module.
  `external_body` on direct callees in dependency modules is expected
  until those modules are verified; **Never** mark callers
  (upstream modules) as `external_body`
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

---

## Proof Organization

- **Write proof helpers in `.proof.rs` from the start.** If a proof block
  would exceed ~5 lines, don't write it inline — define a `proof fn` in the
  `.proof.rs` file and call it from the inline `proof { }` block. Same for
  loop invariants with more than ~5 clauses: define a `spec fn` predicate in
  `.proof.rs` and reference it in the `invariant` clause. This avoids
  cluttering exec code and eliminates extraction work later.
- Keep proof fn granular: one lemma per function, chain via `assert ... by { lemma_call(); }`
- Default: make specs `opaque`, only `reveal()` where needed

## Inductive Invariants

Functions with loops or recursion need inductive invariants — without them
Verus cannot verify the function. If loop invariants already exist, review

---
name: verification-order
description: "Determine function-level verification order within a module using the verification plan. Use at the start of proving to know which function to verify first and how to sequence work."
---

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.
2. **Verify functions in the listed order** (top to bottom = leaves first).
   The first function has no intra-module dependencies; later functions
   may call earlier ones.
3. **Do not skip ahead.** Resolve each function's `admit()` before moving
   to the next. This mirrors the proving-guide's "one function at a time"
   rule but with a concrete ordering.
4. **Cross-module deps** listed in the output tell you which dependency
   modules need specs. If a callee in another module lacks a spec, write
   an `assume_specification` or verify that module first.

## Output Format

```
## kernel::mm::phys::kpool
   crate: kernel  |  file: src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kpool.rs

    #  Function                        Line  In-module deps
  ───  ──────────────────────────────  ─────  ──────────────────────────────
    1  KpoolInner::alloc               L56   —
    2  KernelFrame::deref_mut          L160  —
    3  KernelFrame::clear              L144  KernelFrame::deref_mut
    4  Kpool::alloc                    L205  KpoolInner::alloc, clear
```

Use `-v` to also see cross-module dependency modules.

Functions are ordered so that by the time you reach function N, all its
intra-module dependencies (functions 1..N-1) are already verified.

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Auto-Fixable Bugs

Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.

Auto-fixable categories:
- **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
  checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
- **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
- **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
- **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation

For each auto-fix:
1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
   (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)

Do NOT auto-fix:
- Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
- Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
- Anything requiring architectural changes
- Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches

For these, report only — a human should decide.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
**Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

name: bug-reporting
description: "Classify and report bugs found during Verus verification. Distinguishes true bugs from missing constraints and verifier limitations. Use when a verification failure might indicate a code bug."
---

# Bug Reporting

Finding real code bugs is a high-value outcome of formal verification.
Not every verification failure is a bug — ensure you have genuinely attempted
to prove it first (see `proving-guide`) before classifying a failure as one.

## Classification

After genuinely exhausting proof attempts (see `proving-guide`), classify
every remaining verification failure into one of three categories:

**True Bug** — the code is wrong regardless of calling context. No reasonable
precondition could make it correct (e.g. arithmetic overflow on all inputs,
logic error that always produces wrong results).

**Context-Dependent** — the code looks incorrect in isolation but may be
correct given constraints enforced elsewhere (e.g. callers guarantee bounds,
a system invariant ensures uniqueness). Check callers, upstream module specs,
and system-wide invariants before concluding it's a bug.

**False Positive** — the code is correct but verification fails due to
spec errors (overly strong postcondition, wrong invariant) or solver
limitations (trigger issues, quantifier reasoning gaps).

## When to Report

- **True Bug**: report immediately. This is the highest-value finding.
- **Context-Dependent**: report with analysis of what constraints would be
  needed and where they might come from.
- **False Positive**: do not report — fix the proof approach instead.
  Never weaken existing specs (requires/ensures) to work around a verification
  failure; see `verus-constraints`.

## Auto-Fixable Bugs

Some true bugs are mechanical and can be fixed immediately to unblock
verification. **Fix these directly in the source code** and commit with
the `[verus-ai] BUG FIX:` prefix so the fix is clearly attributed to
verification. Still record them in `bugs.md`.

Auto-fixable categories:
- **Arithmetic overflow/underflow**: missing checked arithmetic or bounds
  checks (e.g. `a + b` → `a.checked_add(b)`, or adding a bounds guard)
- **Off-by-one**: fencepost errors in loop bounds or index calculations
- **Missing bounds check**: index used without prior length/capacity check
- **Unchecked cast**: lossy `as` cast without range validation

For each auto-fix:
1. Make the **minimal** code change that fixes the bug
2. Record the fix in `bugs.md` with full details (see Report Format)
3. Add `// VERUS BUG FIX: <one-line description>` comment at the fix site
4. Re-run AST consistency — the fix is a **pre-approved deviation** (bug fix category)
5. Commit with `git commit --no-verify -m "[verus-ai] BUG FIX: <description>"` message
   (`--no-verify` is required because pre-commit hooks would reject exec changes)

Do NOT auto-fix:
- Algorithmic/design bugs (wrong data structure, incorrect state machine logic)
- Concurrency bugs (race conditions, missing synchronization)
- Anything requiring architectural changes
- Anything where the "fix" is unclear or has multiple valid approaches

For these, report only — a human should decide.

## Report Format

Write findings to the bugs file (path provided in prompt context).
Reports will be read by human developers — use clear language, avoid jargon,
and make each report self-contained so readers need no additional context.

```markdown
## [True Bug | Context-Dependent] — function_name (file.rs:line)

**What**: one-line summary of the issue.
**Why**: root cause analysis — what the code does wrong and why.
**Verification Failure**: which clause failed (requires/ensures/invariant/assert),
verification command, and key error output.
**How Verus Helped**: how formal verification caught this bug (e.g. would it
be caught by testing? code review? why verification was uniquely effective).
**Severity**: safety-critical / correctness / cosmetic.
**Suggested Fix**: how the code should be changed.
**Auto-Fixed**: Yes/No — if yes, describe the exact change made.
```

If no bugs are found, write "None" to the bugs file.

# Verification Order

## Purpose

When proving a module, you must verify functions in **dependency order**:
verify callees before callers. This avoids wasting effort on callers whose
callees don't yet have specs, and ensures each function's dependencies are
already proven when you reach it.

## How to Get the Order

A pre-generated verification plan may exist at:

```
{logs_dir}/verification-plan.json
```

If this file exists, use `show_fn_order.py` to display the function order:

```bash
# Show function order for a specific module
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "kernel::mm::phys::kpool"

# Glob pattern to match multiple modules
python3 {scripts_dir}/show_fn_order.py {logs_dir}/verification-plan.json \
    -m "bitmap::*"
```

If the file does not exist, skip this step and use your best judgment for
function ordering (generally: leaf helpers first, public API functions last).

## How to Use the Order

1. **At the start of proving**, check for the plan and run `show_fn_order.py`.

   may call earlier ones.

# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::new` — wraps a `FrameAddress` into an owning
  kernel-frame handle. Its body calls `crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page`, whose precondition is
  the **global** `identity_map_view().inv()`. That fact is owned by the `mm::virt` identity-map
  ghost token (a parameter-free singleton-global, like `phys_view()`), which is not realized in the
  `mm::phys` module and cannot be derived from the only available precondition (`base.inv()`). So
  the body cannot discharge the callee's `requires` in-scope. Same cross-module global-token
  deferral as `frame::book`/`frame::alloc` (post-mutation `phys_view()`): `external_body` until
  `mm::virt`'s identity-map token is realized, at which point `new` can pass it to
  `identity_map_page` and be verified in-body. `ensures Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv()` (the
  address is preserved and page-aligned); `kframe`'s siblings `base`/`drop` verify in-body.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging` (`mod.rs`)

# TCB Allowed List — Nanvix phys-mm

Any `external_body` outside this list must be removed.

## Allowed `external_body`

- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/frame.rs::instance` — materializes a `&'static mut Inner` from the
  module-level `static mut INSTANCE: MaybeUninit<Inner>` singleton (guarded by `INSTANCE_INIT`).
  Raw-memory op over externally-owned `static mut` storage Verus cannot verify without a
  `PointsTo` (mirrors `bump_allocator`/`raw-array`). `ensures` pins the singleton's abstract
  state to `phys_view().frames`, asserts `(*r).inv()`, and records `phys_view().initialized` —
  the §8 ghost-token attachment for the singleton frame allocator.
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::deref_mut`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::clear`
- `src/kernel/src/mm/phys/kframe.rs::KernelFrame::new` — wraps a `FrameAddress` into an owning
  kernel-frame handle. Its body calls `crate::mm::virt::identity_map_page`, whose precondition is
  the **global** `identity_map_view().inv()`. That fact is owned by the `mm::virt` identity-map
  ghost token (a parameter-free singleton-global, like `phys_view()`), which is not realized in the
  `mm::phys` module and cannot be derived from the only available precondition (`base.inv()`). So
  the body cannot discharge the callee's `requires` in-scope. Same cross-module global-token
  deferral as `frame::book`/`frame::alloc` (post-mutation `phys_view()`): `external_body` until
  `mm::virt`'s identity-map token is realized, at which point `new` can pass it to
  `identity_map_page` and be verified in-body. `ensures Ok(kf) => kf@ == base@ && kf.inv()` (the
  address is preserved and page-aligned); `kframe`'s siblings `base`/`drop` verify in-body.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc` — materializes a
  `&'static mut [u8; N]` from a backend-provided address (`usize as *mut`); raw-memory
  op Verus cannot verify without a `PointsTo` for the externally-owned `BssStorage`
  region. Mirrors `src/libs/raw-array`. `ensures` states alignment + in-bounds over
  the abstract `bump_view`.
- `src/libs/bump_allocator/src/lib.rs::FixedSizeBumpAllocator::alloc_as` — delegates to
  `alloc` and re-materializes the slot as `&'static mut MaybeUninit<T>`; same rationale.
  `ensures` adds the `size_of::<T>()`/`align_of::<T>()` vs `(N, A)` guard arms.

## `external_body` introduced while speccing `arch::x86::mem::paging::table`

- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::read` — reads a `TableEntry` from a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *const E::Word`).
  Verus does not support `usize`→pointer casts (int-to-ptr materialization of externally-owned,
  volatile page-table memory), so the body cannot be verified. Same trust-boundary rationale as
  `bump_allocator::alloc` (`usize as *mut`) and `frame::instance`. See
  `nanvix-phys-arch-paging-table/verus-unsupported.md`. **The function is not contract-free:** it
  carries a full `#[verus_spec]` pinned to the global page-table-memory ghost — `requires index@ <
  PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH`, `ensures result == spec_table_read::<E>(self@.addr, index@)` — exactly as
  `frame::instance` pins its result to `phys_view()` (parameter-free global ghost, no signature
  change).
- `src/libs/arch/src/x86/mem/paging/table.rs::Table::<E>::write` — writes a `TableEntry` into a
  page-table slot through a raw pointer materialized from `self.base` (`usize as *mut E::Word`).
  Same int-to-ptr / volatile externally-owned-memory limitation as `read`. Carries only the sound
  `requires index@ < PAGE_TABLE_LENGTH` (auto from `TableIndex::inv`); it has **no** contents
  `ensures`. A contents postcondition pinning the *pure* global ghost `spec_table_word(self@.addr,
  index@)` to the caller-chosen `entry` would be unsound for an `external_body` (assumed)
  contract: two writes of distinct entries to the same slot would assume
  `spec_entry_raw(e1) == spec_entry_raw(e2)`, which with `lemma_entry_roundtrip` derives
  `e1 == e2`, i.e. `false` (Turn 2 review #2/#3/#15; exploit reproduced). The genuine `old@ -> @`
  slot-update transition (`self@.entries[index@] == Some(entry)`, other slots framed) is therefore
  **deferred to the proving-phase page-table permission token**, exactly the `identity_map_view()`
  `v -> v'` deferral convention in `identity_map.spec.rs`.

# Bugs — `src/kernel/src/hal/mem/types/address/phys.rs`

None.

The verification targets (`from_mmio_address`, `from_number`, `into_frame_number`,
and the `PhysicalAddress` view/`inv`) were all proven without uncovering any code
bug. The two non-trivial proof obligations were genuine proof gaps, not defects:

- `from_number`'s base-address multiply (`frame.into_raw_value() * FRAME_SIZE`) is
  overflow-free because every `FrameNumber` is bounded by `FrameNumber::spec_max()
  == MAX_ADDRESS / FRAME_SIZE - 1`. The bound is supplied by `into_raw_value`'s
  postcondition; `lemma_from_number_no_overflow` closes the arithmetic.
- `into_frame_number`'s `raw_addr >> FRAME_SHIFT` equals `addr / FRAME_SIZE` and
  fits a `FrameNumber` under `inv()`; `lemma_frame_index` discharges this via
  `lemma_usize_shr_is_div`, after deriving `FRAME_SHIFT == 12 < usize::BITS` from
  `spec_page_size() == pow2(FRAME_SHIFT)` (the kernel target is 32-bit, so
  `usize::BITS == 32`).
